endorsements.title: CHAI AI governance frameworks (playbooks)
endorsements.quote: Intended users need explicit education on the difference between recommendation-only AI and action-taking AI, and on the boundaries of the agent's tool access.

commentary.bottom_line: No study supplied tests whether training frontline users to recognize, escalate, halt, or roll back agentic AI actions reduces harm, and no study documents how often users fail to stop harmful agent actions. The recommendation currently rests on a single framework endorsement from CHAI.

perspectives.view: Zero studies test the practice and zero studies document the hazard, so no certainty rating can be assigned. The only support is a CHAI playbook statement rated as a must. Under GRADE conventions, expert framework guidance is an endorsement, not evidence of effect, and it cannot be upgraded or downgraded without data.

No supplied study measures how often users miss or fail to stop harmful autonomous actions, how severe the resulting harm is, or whether training shortens the time to halt or reverse an action. The size of the safety benefit from training therefore remains unknown.

The CHAI framework calls for explicit education on the difference between recommendation-only and action-taking AI and on the limits of an agent's tool access. This is voluntary industry guidance. No federal or state requirement for agent-specific user training appears among the supplied sources.

commentary.research_gap: Studies are needed that compare trained and untrained users in simulated or live agentic AI deployments and measure recognition of agent actions, time to escalation, successful halts and rollbacks, and downstream patient harm. Baseline studies that quantify how often users fail to detect or stop harmful agent actions would also establish whether the hazard is common enough to justify the training burden.
commentary.underserved_note: No study tested the practice, so no evidence covers Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. Health systems cannot yet judge whether training content or halt procedures work equally well for staff and patients in these settings.
